text: movement: The movement in tennis has many many layers to it. There should be reason behind the way a player moves on the tennis court and the reason will depend on numerous aspects. Prioritising speed versus balance: Movement prioritising speed will involve more cross over steps than shuffle steps. And movement prioritising balance will involve more shuffle steps than cross overs. This is due to the direction the player’s hip is facing. Shuffle steps maintain the players hips to face the opponent’s side, providing more balance and readiness to change direction if needed. Cross over steps brings more speed but jeopardises balance. It is important to use both types of movement, and understanding when to use what. Output shot direction: Output shot is cross court: typcially allows the player to recover less to the middle. Output shot quality: When the output shot quality is attackable by the opponent, the player should look to move backwards and get ready to scramble on defence. How much backwards the player should move will depend on the situation, but overall moving backwards to give themself more time on defence. When the output shot quality is of high standard and attacks the opponent, the player should look to move forwards and ready to take on the next ball on offence. How much forwards the player should move will also depend on the situation, but overall look to gain an aggressive position for the next ball. Guesswork on Defence: In order to turn around the momentum of the point, the player can choose to guess which side the opponent will hit to. The guessing of sides and movement should be committed right before the opponent makes contact with the ball, aiming to not show the movement too early. This is a very common movement especially when the player knows without guessing, they will be unable to chase to the ball in time. Diagonal movement to take early or take later: Moving diagonally

Diagonal movement to take early or take later: Moving diagonally forwards can allow players to take a ball on early. This takes time away from the opponent and allows the player to take a better offensive position. Moving diagonally backwards can provide players with more time. This allows the player to have extra time to get in position to hit a quality shot.

serve: Every point in tennis starts off with a serve. It is a vast vast majority of the time hit overhead. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: the dominant hand should be holding a grip on the bottom of the racket grip called the continental or hammer grip while the non-dominant hand holds the ball. Stance: with both feet baseline, the server needs to stand to either side of the centre mark line. Start with both chest and feet pointing to the dominant-side net post. Your dominant foot should be staggered behind the other foot with its toe in line behind the non-dominant heel. The racket swing until trophy position: start with both hands relaxed and down your body. Raise both arms up. The non-dominant hand tosses the ball in front while the dominant arm should bring the racket and create the trophy position and the knees bend into a quarter-squat position. The trophy

serve: non-dominant hand tosses the ball in front while the dominant arm should bring the racket and create the trophy position and the knees bend into a quarter-squat position. The trophy position: the trophy position is the body position of the player typically erected into a trophy. With the non-dominant arm pointing all the way up, the dominant elbow just below shoulder level, racket pointing upwards to the sky and knees bent into a quarter-squat position. Trophy position swing into contact: As the racket drops down the player’s spine and swings up towards the ball, the non-dominant arm should be pulled down and legs should drive the body up and off the ground. Swing until contact: swing the racket directly to the ball. Typically, the racket face should face upwards to the sky, unless the player is swinging downwards at the volley. risk: Understanding risk is a key concept for players who can consistently rally and play points with an opponent. Every shot comes with a certain of risk to take. There is no definitive answer as to when exactly a player should take more or less risk - the player needs to experiment and find what works best for them. A simple starting point will be the scoreline. Leading in score, means more opportunity to take risks, while being behind in score means less opportunity to take risks. And we will break it down into four main types of risk. Risk in terms of court geometry: The tennis court is a rectangle, with a net that is lowest in the middle and heightens towards the sidelines. Using these facts about the tennis court, we can distinguish the risks being taken among these three shot directions: cross-court, down the line, and middle. Playing

risk: heightens towards the sidelines. Using these facts about the tennis court, we can distinguish the risks being taken among these three shot directions: cross-court, down the line, and middle. Playing shots middle offers players the least amount of risk in multiple ways: the net is lower in the middle, the middle area is a lot larger and forgiving, and the opponent will have less angle to work with. Playing shots cross court involves hitting the ball diagonally across the net. Cross court is mid level of risk. It utilises the lower part of the net and still a sizable target area. But opens the court angles up for the opponent. Playing shots down the line is where the player hits the ball straight and parallel to the sideline over the higher part of the net. risk: the ball straight and parallel to the sideline over the higher part of the net. This shot involves higher risk due to the net height, smaller target area and giving the opponent more room to hit into. Risk in terms of contact heights with the ball: We can break down the height of contact into 3 sections: below hip level, hip to shoulder height, and shoulder to head height. The risk of shots being played at different heights will vary amongst different shots depending on grips, movement and more. This is a general guide. Contact below hip level: tends to be the riskiest height of the three. The player will need to clear the net with enough spin and height, whilst ensuring it’s not overdone resulting in hitting the ball out. Player’s seem to be able to balance spin and power better at this height. Contact between shoulder and head height: tends to be middle risk. The net is no longer a major concern, however overhitting becomes more likely. A player’s perception of whether a ball is accelerating or decelerating is up to their discretion, level, and experience. We will pair up this section with incoming and outputting ball speeds. Since the shot from the opponent is already accelerating, further accelerating your own shot can lead to losing control a lot of the time. Accelerating incoming and decelerating outputting: is a lower risk combination. By deccelerating the incoming faster shot, we are able to control the ball better, reducing chances of an error being made. Since the incoming ball is of slower speed, accelerating your own shot is a good choice as it can help the player gain offensive advantage and doesn’t pose too much of a risk as the a slower incoming ball gives the player more time to prepare. Risk in terms of movement: We will break this section down into movement after the incoming ball is hit versus before the incoming ball is hit. Both types of movement should be used as they provide different benefits. Moving after the incoming ball is hit: is a lower risk play as the player does not need to do much guess work. And the racket face should mostly face upwards on the follow through, unless the player had to swing downwards at the volley. Racket should not be swung across the body to finish the shot. Footwork: when able to, it is preferred to step with a forehand volley. Which foot steps and the direction of the step will depend on the incoming shot. When the player has time to move forwards to play the volley they will step forwards

forehand volley: foot steps and the direction of the step will depend on the incoming shot. When the player has time to move forwards to play the volley they will step forwards and across with his non-dominant side foot when swinging at the volley. All other variations and combinations can work depending on the situation. COMMON MISTAKES: Hitting the ball too flat or in the net: normally caused by the racket face at contact being too closed off and not pointing enough to the sky. This can also be caused by the swing going downwards too much. Fix: open the racket face up at contact more for a higher ball flight path. And adjusting the swing motion based on the height of contact. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: normally caused by overswinging and/or not adjusting the racket face for contact point. Fix: keep the volley swing compact and not

Fix: keep the volley swing compact and not swinging across the body. People also swing too hard, so slow the swing speed down. Depending on the volley, some may need to open or close the racket face more at contact. Hitting the ball out in terms of width: caused by the player contacting the ball too early or late and/or hitting the ball at an extreme angle. Fix: Keeping the racket face at contact point facing towards the targeted spot on court. And try to find a contact point not too early and not too late. Late contact with the ball: when the ball flies past the hip before contact point. The player would feel like they are making contact very close to their body and their hitting

The player would feel like they are making contact very close to their body and their hitting elbow very close to the body at contact. Fix: prepare the arms as soon as the player sees the ball fly towards their forehand and think about making contact as early as you can. And taking a step when swinging the volley will help as well. Mishitting the ball: when the ball hits the player’s racket frame instead of the strings. Fix: tracking the ball all the way to the contact point. The player should also give themself sufficient space between the contact point. Keep their head still and volley through the ball.

forehand slice: A forehand slice is a shot that is hit on the player’s dominant side after one bounce. Unlike a topspin forehand, a slice forehand aims to cause the ball to spin sideways or backwards. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: holding the continental, aka hammer grip with the dominant hand at the bottom of the grip. Preparation: unit turn with both arms, chest should be facing towards the player’s dominant side of the court, racket up by the side of the player’s head and non-dominant hand by the throat of the racket. Swing until contact: swing the racket towards the ball. In many instances, the swing will involve dropping underneath the ball but not always. Unlike a topspin forehand, we do not need to “brush” the ball on the slice. Contact: most of the time, during contact with the ball, the racket should be facing somewhat upwards. This will depend on what the

forehand slice: to “brush” the ball on the slice. Contact: most of the time, during contact with the ball, the racket should be facing somewhat upwards. This will depend on what the player is aiming to achieve with the slice. The contact point should be in front of the player’s hips preferably with the hitting elbow away from the player’s body. Follow through: there should be a follow through after contact. And the racket face should mostly face upwards on the follow through. Racket should not be swung across the body to finish the shot. The length of the follow through will depend on what the player wishes to achieve with the shot in terms of length, spin, and speed. Can also be caused by not dropping the racket underneath the ball enough prior to contact. Fix: open the racket face up at contact more for a higher ball flight path. And adjusting the swing motion based on the height of contact. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: normally caused by overswinging and/or not adjusting the racket face for contact point. Fix: Keeping the racket face at contact point facing towards the targeted spot on court. And try to find a contact point not too early and not too late. The player would feel like they are making contact very close to their body and their hitting elbow very close to the body at contact. Fix: prepare the arms as soon as the player sees the ball fly towards their forehand and think about making contact as early as you can. Mishitting the ball: when the ball hits the player’s racket frame instead of the strings. Fix: tracking the ball all the way to the contact point. The player should also give themself sufficient space between the contact point. Keep their head still and swing through the ball. Forehand slice is floating up too much: is caused by the racket face being too open at contact and therefore hitting too much underneath the ball. Fix: think about hitting behind the ball first, then opening the racket face up after. By contacting behind the ball first, the player is able to cause the ball to fly forwards instead of upwards. Then opening the racket face up will give the ball the spin needed.
forehand slice: ball to fly forwards instead of upwards. Then opening the racket face up will give the ball the spin needed.

forehand return of serve: The forehand return of serve is the shot hit off the opponents serve. It is hit on the player’s dominant side after one bounce. KEY CHECKPOINTS FOR TOPSPIN FOREHAND RETURN OF SERVE: Grip: Semi-western for most players. Hold the grip palm down, pretending to flip on egg on a pan Preparation: Since we have a lot less time on the return of serve, the preparation should be abbreviated. Still aim to have a unit turn, but think of only performing 50% of the normal forehand take back. Swing to contact point: let the racket drop down and swing towards the ball. As the racket swings towards the ball, the non-dominant arm should pull itself towards the body and finish on the players chest Contact point: the contact point should have the racket face facing either straight to the ball or slightly closed downwards. It should not face upwards to the

forehand return of serve: the players chest Contact point: the contact point should have the racket face facing either straight to the ball or slightly closed downwards. It should not face upwards to the sky at all. Ideally the contact point should be in front of the body, with the dominant arm’s elbow away from the body Follow through: After contact, the racket arm should be extended out towards where the player is aiming and eventually wrap around the non-dominant side of the body. The follow through should have the racket face that made contact with the ball, facing the non-dominant side of the player. For example, the racket face should finish facing to the left side of a right handed player. The dominant elbow should finish towards the centre line of the body and away from it. The height of where the follow through finishes depends on how much spin and arc is

forehand return of serve: elbow should finish towards the centre line of the body and away from it. The height of where the follow through finishes depends on how much spin and arc is wanted of the shot. Lower finish means less arc and spin, higher finish means more arc and spin. Footwork: the player should be split stepping before hitting the return of serve. This involves a small jump right before the opponent makes contact with the ball. The player should aim to land the same time as the opponent makes contact. This way the player is able to be balanced and ready to return serves on both sides of their body. The first step after the split step includes stepping the same side foot outwards. The second step should be a bigger step going across and forwards with the other foot. As that step lands, contact should be made with the ball.

forehand return of serve: side foot outwards. The second step should be a bigger step going across and forwards with the other foot. As that step lands, contact should be made with the ball. And the third step involves a balancing step going outside with the same side foot. Overall, the entire movement should involve moving diagonally forwards to the shot. The player should end with the dominant side foot in line or in front of the non-dominant side foot. COMMON MISTAKES FOR TOPSPIN FOREHAND RETURN OF SERVE: Hitting the ball too flat or in the net: normally caused by the swing path being too horizontal or flat. Fix: when dropping the racket, think about dropping the hand below the height of the ball to ensure the swing starts at a low enough point. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: normally caused by the racket face at contact facing the sky, and/or

forehand return of serve: to ensure the swing starts at a low enough point. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: normally caused by the racket face at contact facing the sky, and/or not completing the follow through. Fix: hit and brush over the ball while following through Hitting the ball out in terms of width: caused by the player throwing their body around at contact and/or hitting the ball at an extreme angle. Fix: keeping the chest straight on with the ball at contact and think about the racket face should face where the player is aiming at contact. Late contact with the ball: when the ball flies past the hip before contact. The player would feel like they are making contact very close to their body. Fix: prepare the arms early, as soon as the player sees the ball fly towards their forehand and begin the swing earlier. Ensure a smaller

forehand return of serve: very close to their body. Fix: prepare the arms early, as soon as the player sees the ball fly towards their forehand and begin the swing earlier. Ensure a smaller preparation for the return of serve. Mishitting the ball: when the ball hits the player’s racket frame instead of the strings. Fix: tracking the ball all the way to contact and watching the racket make contact with the ball. Keep the head and chest still at contact and hit through the ball. Another great cue is to keep the chest side on for longer during contact. This prevents the player from throwing their torso at contact, which frequently leads to mishitting the ball.

balance: BALANCE AND MOVEMENT — FOUNDATION PHILOSOPHY Everything starts with balanced movement. Without balance, everything else the student performs is redundant. A balanced player can correctly position themselves relative to the ball and perform complex actions to manipulate it. Balance is taught before any technique — a student must be able to move with balance before they swing at the ball. PROGRESSION — complete each before moving on: 1. Student moves to the ball with balance, no swing. 2. Student balances on both feet whilst hitting. 3. Student balances on either foot whilst hitting. WHAT BALANCED MOVEMENT LOOKS LIKE: - Chest upright before, during, and after the shot. - Head still — eyes track the ball all the way to racket contact, not lifting early to see where the ball goes. - Weight on balls of feet, knees slightly bent in ready position. - After the shot, player can hold their

balance: contact, not lifting early to see where the ball goes. - Weight on balls of feet, knees slightly bent in ready position. - After the shot, player can hold their finish position without stumbling. COMMON BALANCE ERRORS IN TENNIS: - Moving feet, torso or head during the swing: caused by late positioning — the student is still arriving at the ball when they swing, so the body is still in motion. Fix: get there early, stop, then swing. - Torso collapsing after the shot: caused by rushing to recover before finishing the swing, or weak. core engagement through contact. Fix: think about finishing the shot before recovering back. CUES FOR BALANCE: - "Hold your finish until the your shot bounces" - "Pretend you're standing on a surfboard — stay centred" - "Move your feet, then swing — not at the same time" DRILLS FOR BALANCE: Drill 1 — Stop and

balance: - "Pretend you're standing on a surfboard — stay centred" - "Move your feet, then swing — not at the same time" DRILLS FOR BALANCE: Drill 1 — Stop and Swing: Coach feeds balls to various positions. Student must move to the ball, stop both feet completely, swing, and freeze the finish position until the ball lands on the other side. If the student moves during the swing the rep doesn't count. Start slow, increase feed pace as balance improves.

smashes: A smash is also called an overhead or an overhead smash. It is a shot hit above the player’s head just like a serve, and can either be hit before the ball bounces or after one bounce. KEY CHECKPOINTS: Grip: the dominant hand should be holding a grip on the bottom of the racket grip called the continental or hammer grip. Stance and preparation: as soon as the player recognises the opportunity to hit a overhead smash, they should begin preparing the arms and move their feet into position. Start with both chest facing the to the dominant-side. The non-dominant arm should be pointing upwards towards the ball. The dominant elbow should be positions behind the dominant shoulder, with its elbow spaced away from the body while being under shoulder height. The racket should be pointing up towards the sky. Combining all these, the player should be creating a ‘trophy

smashes: elbow spaced away from the body while being under shoulder height. The racket should be pointing up towards the sky. Combining all these, the player should be creating a ‘trophy position’. Optimally, the player should be in the position to step forwards into the overhead smash but won’t be able to all the time. Trophy position swing into contact: As the racket drops down the player’s spine and swings up towards the ball, the non-dominant arm should be pulled down. If able to, push the dominant side hip and the legs should drive the body up and off the ground. Contact: should be made with the entire body extended upwards, chest stays up, and dominant arm fully extended with the racket. Different ways of contact cause a different spin to occur to the ball. The player should feel a sense of pronation when hitting the overhead smash. Follow through: after

smashes: racket. Different ways of contact cause a different spin to occur to the ball. The player should feel a sense of pronation when hitting the overhead smash. Follow through: after contact, the racket should finish down by the lower half of the non-dominant side of the body. Footwork: for overhead smashes moving forwards, shuffle up to the ball and step the non-dominant foot in as the last step into the smash. For overhead smashes moving backwards, cross over steps and the player should jump off their dominant side foot to hit and land behind on their non-dominant side foot. COMMON MISTAKES: Hitting the ball in the net: caused by the body not driving upwards during the overhead smash, or swinging downwards too much. Fix: The player should aim to keep their chest up tall at contact and chin up at finish. And aim to swing up first at the ball.

smashes: downwards too much. Fix: The player should aim to keep their chest up tall at contact and chin up at finish. And aim to swing up first at the ball. Hitting the ball out in terms of length: caused by hitting under the ball during the overhead smash. Fix: The player should aim to hit the ‘top’ of the ball at contact. This fix may involve contacting the ball higher so the racket arm can extend up. Hitting the ball out in terms of width: caused by the player throwing their body around at contact and/or hitting the ball at an extreme angle. Fix: keeping the chest facing the ball at contact and the racket face should face where the player is aiming at contact.
